subject: English
topic: Sentence Improvement — Correct the Underlined Part (W11 B1)

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part:
'She is more better at mathematics than her brother.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'More better' is a double comparative — using 'more' with an already comparative form ('better') is redundant and incorrect. 'Better' is already the comparative of 'good'. Correct: 'She is BETTER at mathematics than her brother.' Trap: 'More good' is also wrong — the comparative of 'good' is 'better', not 'more good'; 'most better' is doubly wrong (superlative + comparative mixed).

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part:
'He told me that he has been waiting for two hours.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. In indirect speech with a past reporting verb ('told'), the tense backshifts: Present Perfect Continuous ('has been waiting') → Past Perfect Continuous ('had been waiting'). 'He told me that he HAD BEEN WAITING for two hours.' Trap: 'is waiting' = Present Continuous (no backshift at all — wrong); 'was waiting' = Past Continuous (backshift of Present Continuous, not Present Perfect Continuous — incomplete); 'No improvement' = wrong since backshift is required.

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part:
'Neither of the two solutions were satisfactory.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Neither' takes a singular verb. 'Neither of the two solutions WAS satisfactory.' Rule: neither/either/each/one → singular verb regardless of the noun that follows. Trap: 'are satisfactory' = present tense plural (wrong on both counts — wrong tense and wrong number); 'have been satisfactory' = plural present perfect (wrong number); 'No improvement' = wrong, since 'were' is incorrect with 'neither'.

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part:
'I prefer tea more than coffee.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Prefer' takes 'to', NOT 'more than'. The correct construction is: 'prefer X TO Y'. 'I prefer tea TO coffee.' Trap: 'rather than' is used with 'would prefer' (not plain 'prefer'): 'I would prefer tea rather than coffee' — but with plain 'prefer', use 'to'; 'over' is informal American English usage but not standard in Indian/British formal tests; 'more than' with 'prefer' is the classic SSC error tested frequently.

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part:
'One should always respect his elders.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. When 'one' is the subject, the pronoun referring back to it should be 'one's' (not 'his', 'their', or 'our'). 'One should always respect ONE'S elders.' Rule: 'one → one's → oneself'. Using 'his' after 'one' is an older usage that is now considered incorrect in standard formal English. Trap: 'their' = gender-neutral plural pronoun (acceptable in casual use but 'one's' is the grammatically consistent formal choice with 'one'); 'our' = first person plural (inconsistent with third-person 'one').

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part:
'The jury was divided on their verdict.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Jury' is a collective noun. When the members act individually (divided opinion), it takes a plural verb. 'The jury WERE divided' (individual disagreement). Additionally, if plural verb 'were' is used, the pronoun should be plural 'their'. So 'The jury WERE divided on THEIR verdict.' Trap: 'was divided on its verdict' = treats jury as singular unit (correct only when they act unanimously, not when 'divided'); 'were divided on its verdict' = inconsistent: plural 'were' but singular 'its'; 'No improvement' = wrong since the original has a concord problem.

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part:
'I have met him last Tuesday.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Last Tuesday' is a specific past time reference. With a specific past time marker, Simple Past is used, NOT Present Perfect. 'I MET him last Tuesday.' The error: 'have met' (Present Perfect) + 'last Tuesday' (specific past time) is incorrect. Present Perfect must not be used with specific past time expressions ('last week/month/year', 'yesterday', 'in 2020', 'at 5 PM'). Trap: 'had met' = Past Perfect (used for event before another past event — no second past event mentioned); 'was meeting' = Past Continuous (suggests interrupted action).

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part:
'The number of road accidents are increasing every year.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'THE NUMBER OF' takes a singular verb. 'The number of road accidents IS increasing.' Contrast: 'A NUMBER OF' takes a plural verb ('A number of students ARE absent'). Rule: 'the number' = singular; 'a number' = plural. Trap: 'have been increasing' = plural Present Perfect Continuous (wrong verb number); 'were increasing' = past tense (wrong tense and wrong number); 'No improvement' = wrong.

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part:
'The teacher asked the students to open their books and explained the lesson.'

options.option_text: and explained the lesson to them

questions.explanation: D is correct. The sentence is grammatically correct. 'The teacher asked the students to open their books and EXPLAINED the lesson.' Two actions of the teacher: (1) 'asked [them] to open their books' and (2) 'explained the lesson' — both are past tense verbs with 'The teacher' as subject. The parallel structure is correct: 'asked...and explained.' Trap: 'and to explain' would make the explaining part of what the teacher asked students to do (students explain, not teacher — wrong meaning); 'and explaining' breaks the tense parallel.

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part:
'He works very hardly to support his family.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Hard' can function as both an adjective AND an adverb. The adverbial form of 'hard' is 'hard' (not 'hardly'). 'He works very HARD.' HARDLY is a different word meaning 'scarcely/barely' ('He hardly works' = he barely works — opposite meaning!). Trap: 'hardly' = scarcely (completely changes the meaning — a classic SSC trap); 'hardily' is not a standard English word in this context; 'harder' = comparative form (wrong — no comparison being made).
